name: Limostatin
lead: Limostatin (Lst) is a peptide hormone first identified in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster. It is released from gut-associated endocrine cells when nutrients are scarce and suppresses the production and secretion of insulin-like peptides, which made it the first well-characterised example of a "decretin", a fasting-induced hormone that opposes insulin.[1][5]

All published work on limostatin consists of insect or cell-based laboratory research. Flies lacking the gene showed high insulin levels, low blood sugar and extra body fat in the original 2015 study.[1] No human trial of limostatin or a limostatin-based product has been reported, and no source reviewed for this article documents its use for appearance or body-composition goals in humans.[1][2]
infobox: Suppresses insulin secretion under nutrient restriction

paras: Researchers identified limostatin through genetic screens in Drosophila and reported it in 2015 as a hormone induced by nutrient restriction in gut-associated endocrine cells. Loss of the limostatin gene led to hyperinsulinemia, hypoglycemia and excess adiposity in the flies, and a conserved 15-residue peptide encoded by the gene suppressed insulin secretion.[1] The name refers to Limos, the Greek goddess of starvation.[5]

Reviews of insect lipid metabolism and of fly gut-brain signalling place limostatin among the peptide hormones that coordinate fat storage and energy use between the gut, the insulin-producing cells and the fat body.[2][6]

A 2024 study in Drosophila reported that limostatin and its proposed human ortholog promoted West Nile virus infection, linking the peptide to insulin/IGF-1 signalling and immune responses.[3] A 2026 paper described limostatin as an enterokine, produced by a small group of larval midgut enteroendocrine cells, that helps coordinate developmental pace when amino acids are restricted.[4]
No studies found. Research on limostatin is limited to Drosophila and related laboratory models.[1][3][4]

timeline.event: Limostatin reported as a fasting-induced decretin hormone in Drosophila.[1]
Study links fly limostatin and a human ortholog to West Nile virus infection in flies.[3]
Limostatin described as a nutrient-sensitive enterokine coordinating larval developmental plasticity.[4]

card.summary: A fruit-fly hormone that switches insulin down during fasting; studied only in insects, with no human data.
card.note: Fly-only research; no human studies exist.

quick.overview:
Limostatin is a signalling peptide discovered in fruit flies. When food is scarce, it tells insulin-producing cells to release less insulin.

It appears in fat-loss and metabolism peptide lists because of this insulin-lowering role, but the published work is confined to flies and laboratory models.
quick.mechanism: In flies, gut endocrine cells release limostatin during nutrient restriction, and it acts on insulin-producing cells to suppress insulin production and secretion.[1]
quick.risks: No human safety or efficacy data have been published. Flies lacking limostatin developed high insulin, low blood sugar and excess fat, but this has not been tested in people.[1]
